title: Martin Luther King Forgives His Attacker
text:
On September 20, 1958, Martin Luther King Jr. was signing copies of his first book, Stride Toward Freedom, at Blumstein's department store in Harlem, New York. A woman named Izola Ware Curry stepped up, asked if he was Martin Luther King, and stabbed him in the chest with a steel letter opener.

The blade lodged next to his aorta. King sat calmly with it in his chest while he was taken to Harlem Hospital, where surgeons worked for hours to remove it. They later told him that if he had sneezed, he could have died.

Curry, who had a history of mental illness, was found unfit to stand trial and committed to a state hospital. From his hospital bed he issued a statement saying he felt no ill will toward her and hoped she would get the help she needed to become a constructive member of society.

Ten years later, in his last speech in Memphis, King recalled a letter from a young girl who wrote that she was glad he had not sneezed.
lesson: Answering an attack without hatred protects more than your peace of mind. It keeps your cause, and your example to others, free of the bitterness you are fighting against.
people: Martin Luther King Jr., Izola Ware Curry
source: Martin Luther King Jr., statement of September 1958, The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr., vol. 4; King, speech "I've Been to the Mountaintop" (April 3, 1968)
